rep.angle: lead with a peer company's result
rep.name: Arjun

turns.speaker: buyer
turns.text: Hey, Marcus here. You've got about twenty minutes.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.text: Thanks, Marcus. A similar fintech spotted discovery gaps by week two instead of month six. What’s driving Ledgerline’s seven-month AE ramp today?

turns.speaker: buyer
turns.text: Mostly the product is technical. New AEs tend to fumble ERP integration and implementation questions, which costs them credibility on calls.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.text: Got it. How are new AEs practicing those conversations today, and when do managers typically catch the gaps?

turns.speaker: buyer
turns.text: Mostly shadowing and roleplaying with a manager, when schedules allow. In practice, gaps get caught after a live call goes sideways—how is what you do actually different from manager roleplay?

turns.speaker: rep
turns.text: It complements manager roleplay with on-demand buyer practice and scores citing exact quotes. How often do those live-call misses happen?

turns.speaker: buyer
turns.text: I don’t have a clean number; Rachel would. Anecdotally, it comes up most weeks, usually with newer reps on ERP integrations.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.text: When a newer rep loses credibility on ERP integrations, does that usually mean extra technical support, delayed deals, or both?

turns.speaker: buyer
turns.text: Both. We pull in technical people to recover, and sometimes the deal stalls.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.text: That sounds costly. Roughly how much technical time goes into those recoveries, and what would reps need to handle independently to shorten ramp?

turns.speaker: buyer
turns.text: A few hours per deal between prep, follow-up calls, and cleanup, though I haven’t quantified it. Reps need to handle common ERP, API, and implementation questions accurately, then know when to bring in solutions engineering.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.text: That’s the use case: practice ERP, API, and implementation scenarios, with quote-backed scoring on accuracy and escalation. Would a 30-day pilot with Rachel make sense?

turns.speaker: buyer
turns.text: Rachel owns this, not me. A pilot might make sense, but how does that actually work—what data do you need, who builds the scenarios, and what would Rachel see at the end?

turns.speaker: rep
turns.text: We use your materials and call examples to build scenarios together. Rachel sees weekly improvement, recurring gaps, and quote-backed scores; could you connect us?

turns.speaker: buyer
turns.text: Potentially, but customer-call transcripts are sensitive. Do you need recordings to run the pilot, and how are the data stored, retained, and used for model training?
